Slides (black — the unified 453 deck; slides 19–32 are blank), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from the lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no cleft chapter.

  • Cleft lip ± cleft palate is a common congenital craniofacial deformity, in three forms: cleft lip alone (always the upper lip; mainly cosmetic/psychosocial, mild feeding difficulty) · cleft palate alone (oral–nasal communication → feeding, speech, ear and dental problems) · combined (each repaired at its own age window).
  • For every case cover five principles: risk factors · anatomic defect · health effects · treatment · timing of surgery.

1. Causes

  • Unknown · advanced parental age · family history · smoking · medications · associated syndromes.
  • Most cases are idiopathic. Family history is the most important identifiable risk factor: general population < 1% → one affected first-degree relative 2–4% → two affected family members ~7%.
  • Others: advanced parental age · maternal smoking · syndromes/craniofacial abnormalities including Down syndrome · 1st-trimester medications — antineoplastics and anticonvulsants. Nutrition (folate, protein) was mentioned but not emphasized. Exam move: lead with family history, then add maternal smoking or 1st-trimester anticonvulsants.
Added explanationEmbryology: the lip and primary palate (the premaxilla in front of the incisive foramen) form at about 4–7 weeks; the secondary palate (hard and soft palate behind it) fuses at about 8–12 weeks.
  • Gestational age when the primary palate develops → 4–8 weeks. 434 ×2

2. Cleft lip

  • Unilateral / bilateral · complete / incomplete.

Unilateral cleft lip — incomplete (partial) vs complete

  • Always the upper lip. Classify on two axes: side — unilateral (right or left) or bilateral (symmetrical or asymmetrical); extent — incomplete = doesn't reach the nose; complete = extends all the way to the nose.
  • Image question: give the full diagnosis — side + extent + "cleft lip" (e.g. left unilateral complete cleft lip). Closed mouth → describe the lip only; open mouth with the palate visible → lip + palate. Don't comment on the palate unless it is shown.
  • Commoner patterns: unilateral > bilateral · left > right · incomplete > complete.
  • Most common site → left. 436

Defect & clinical impact

  • Defect: skin · mucosa · orbicularis oris · nasal cartilage.
  • Clinical impact: feeding (difficult to make a proper seal) · psychosocial.
  • Key muscle: orbicularis oris. Nasal cartilage is present but hypoplastic/displaced — abnormal nostril shape.
  • Isolated cleft lip: cosmetic/psychosocial is the main problem; feeding mildly affected (poor seal — usually managed with appropriate nipples); speech and hearing not significantly affected.

Management

  • Education (proper feeding: special nipple, feeding upright, frequent feeds).
  • Surgery — cleft lip repair at the age of 3–6 months. Rule of 10s: weight 10 lbs · Hb 10 · 10 weeks.
  • Why 3–6 months: before ~3 months — avoid unnecessary very early surgery, let the infant grow and identify other problems; after ~6 months — the child becomes mobile and moves to solids, so post-op care is harder. Delayed repair can still give a similar result.
  • Rule of 10s (top yield): age ≥ 10 weeks · weight ≥ 10 lb (≈ 4.5 kg) · Hb ≥ 10 g/dL — weight and Hb are markers of overall health and nutrition. Failing it → think malnutrition (often from poor feeding technique) or an underlying medical problem.
  • Surgical principle: reconstruct the lip in layers — mucosa, orbicularis oris, skin; partial correction of the nasal deformity. Definitive rhinoplasty is postponed — aggressive early rhinoplasty scars and interferes with nasal/facial growth.
  • Baby with a cleft palate, feeding problems and poor weight gain (5 kg) — to prepare for surgery → insert a nasogastric tube (secure nutrition). 436
Source key vs the lecture: a bilateral complete cleft with a very short columella and small prolabium at 4 months was keyed "bony alveolus" as the hardest part. The alveolar bone gap is not repaired at 4 months — it is bone-grafted when the canines erupt (the same exam's next question). The stem's clue is the nose: in bilateral clefts the short columella makes nasal correction the most difficult part. Answer here: nasal position.
  • 4-month-old, bilateral complete cleft, very short columella, small prolabium — most difficult part of the repair → nasal position (columella/nose). 436

3. Cleft palate

  • Bifid uvula · soft palate only · soft and hard palate · combined cleft lip and palate.

Submucous cleft palate with bifid uvula · cleft of the soft palate · cleft of the hard and soft palate

  • A cleft palate runs posterior → anterior: uvula → soft palate → hard palate → alveolar/anterior region. No useful unilateral/bilateral classification (unlike the lip). Soft palate = posterior, no bone; hard palate = anterior, bony.
  • Defect: oral mucosa · nasal mucosa · tensor veli palatini muscle · bone (maxilla).

Cleft palate — clinical photo and drawing of the oral–nasal communication

  • Main function of the palate: separate the oral from the nasal cavity. The cleft separates the mucosal layers (oral–nasal communication), leaves the palatal muscles discontinuous/abnormally attached, and anterior clefts may have bony deficiency. Surgical implication: the palatal muscle must be repaired, not just the mucosa closed.

Clinical impact

  • Feeding (unable to make a proper seal, weak swallowing, nasal regurgitation) · speech abnormalities · repeated ear infections · dental · facial growth.
DomainMechanismResultManagement
FeedingNo seal; ineffective swallowing/suctionNasal regurgitation, poor feedingSpecial nipples, upright, small frequent feeds
SpeechAir escapes into the noseSpeech abnormalitiesSpeech therapy
Ear / hearingPalatal dysfunction disturbs middle-ear pressureRecurrent middle-ear infectionsENT follow-up
DentalAbnormal palate/alveolusDental problemsDentistry
  • Multidisciplinary team: plastic/cleft surgery · speech therapy · ENT · dentistry.

Management

  • Education (special nipple, feeding upright, frequent feeds) · surgery — cleft palate repair at the age of 12–18 months.
  • Timing (top yield): 12–18 months — before significant speech development (~2 years). Later → the child learns abnormal compensatory speech habits that persist. Much earlier → the mouth is too small for exposure and instruments (some can be done at ~10 months).
  • Surgical principle: raise flaps from both sides → mobilize medially → reconstruct the palatal musculature → close in layers. Speech after repair improves but may not normalize — the muscles were abnormal; continued speech therapy may be needed.
  • Most important factor in deciding cleft palate surgery → dental and mouth examination (the mouth/palate must be big enough; age 12–18 months is the guide). 436
Added explanationVelopharyngeal insufficiency (VPI) — after palate repair the soft palate may still fail to close off the nasopharynx during speech → hypernasal speech and nasal air escape not fixed by exercises → speech assessment (nasendoscopy) and a secondary operation (pharyngoplasty or pharyngeal flap). Alveolar bone grafting of the alveolar cleft is done in mixed dentition, before the permanent canine erupts (~8–11 years), so the canine can come through grafted bone.
  • 5-year-old after palate repair with nasal speech not responding to exercises → velopharyngeal insufficiency. 436
  • Timing of bone grafting in cleft palate → when the canine teeth come out. 436
